cards.title: Repository: Collection-Like Abstraction Over Persistence
cards.teaser: A Repository provides the illusion that your aggregate roots live in an in-memory collection. Callers add objects, retrieve them by identity or criteria, and remove them — without ever knowing whether the backing store is a relational database, a document store, or a test double.

runs.text: Eric Evans introduced the Repository pattern in
Domain-Driven Design
(2003) as the bridge between the pure domain model and the persistence infrastructure. The defining metaphor is a
collection
: from the caller's perspective, a Repository behaves like a Set or List of aggregate roots that happens to survive process restart.
The Repository pattern has two responsibilities. First, it
hides the mechanics
of persistence — SQL, ORM sessions, connection pools, and cache layers are implementation details invisible to the domain. Second, it
speaks the domain language
: a method called
findActiveCustomersOver18()
expresses business intent; a naked SQL query does not.

items.text: — the Repository is the only place in the domain layer that knows about tables, collections, or indexes. Everything outside the Repository deals only with aggregate objects.
— repository method names are coined using Ubiquitous Language. The interface is part of the domain model, even if the implementation is in the infrastructure layer.
— because a Repository is declared as an interface, unit tests can substitute an in-memory implementation without touching a real database.

runs.text: Evans: "A Repository represents all objects of a certain type as a conceptual set. It acts like a collection, except with more elaborate querying capability." (DDD, ch. 6)

A Repository makes your database look like a plain in-memory collection to the rest of your code. You add things to it, find things in it, and remove things from it — it handles the database details so domain code does not have to.

cards.title: One Repository per Aggregate Root
cards.teaser: DDD mandates exactly one Repository per aggregate root — not per entity, not per database table. This granularity enforces the aggregate boundary and prevents the persistence layer from fragmenting a cluster of related objects that must be treated as one.

runs.text: An aggregate is a cluster of objects — one root Entity plus any child Entities and Value Objects — that must be persisted and retrieved as a unit to enforce its invariants. The Repository operates on the aggregate root because the root is the only entry point to the cluster.
The one-Repository-per-root rule has two concrete implications:

and navigate. If a non-root object needs its own Repository, that is a signal it should be an aggregate root itself.
The Repository loads the whole aggregate.

runs.text: Identifying aggregate boundaries is therefore a prerequisite for designing repositories. If you find yourself wanting a
LineItemRepository
, the question is: have you drawn the aggregate boundary correctly?
The proliferation of fine-grained Repositories — one per database table — is the most common sign that the persistence model has leaked into the domain model. Tables are not aggregates.

Each aggregate gets exactly one Repository, and that Repository deals with the whole cluster. Child objects inside the aggregate don't get their own Repositories — that would break the aggregate boundary.

cards.title: Collection-Oriented vs Persistence-Oriented Interfaces
cards.teaser: There are two schools of Repository interface design: collection-oriented (add/remove, no explicit save) and persistence-oriented (save/delete on every mutation). The choice reveals how much the implementation is leaking into the contract.

runs.text: Vaughn Vernon, in
Implementing Domain-Driven Design
(2013), distinguishes two styles. The difference is visible in a single method: do you call
add()
or
save()

items.text: — the Repository tracks every aggregate it returns (via an identity map or change-tracking). Calling
inserts it. Modifying a retrieved aggregate is enough — the Repository detects changes and persists them at commit time. There is no explicit
. This is the most domain-pure style.
method that must be called explicitly after mutation. This leaks persistence semantics into the domain but is simpler to implement and the default behavior of most ORMs and document stores.

runs.text: The collection-oriented style is purer but requires either ORM-level change tracking (Hibernate, EF Core) or an explicit unit-of-work pattern. The persistence-oriented style is pragmatic — it works with any database driver, at the cost of making persistence visible at the call site.
Choose collection-oriented when your ORM gives you change tracking for free. Choose persistence-oriented when you value simplicity and your persistence mechanism has no identity map.

Collection-oriented means you just add, find, and remove — like a List. Persistence-oriented means you have to call save() explicitly every time you change something. The first is cleaner but harder to implement; the second is simpler but shows the database through the interface.

cards.title: Common Repository Methods
cards.teaser: A well-designed repository interface is small — findById, save (or add), delete, and count are the core four. Everything else is a custom finder that belongs in the domain, named after intent rather than table columns.

Several things are deliberately absent from the minimal interface:

items.text: — returning every aggregate is almost never safe in production. Use a specific finder or a paginated query.
— loading a partial aggregate violates the aggregate boundary contract.
— raw query access lives in the infrastructure implementation, not the domain interface.

runs.text: The Repository interface lives in the domain layer. The implementation lives in the infrastructure layer. Dependency Inversion Principle: the domain declares what it needs; infrastructure fulfills it.

The core Repository needs only four things: find by ID, save, delete, and count. Anything extra should be a named method that expresses a business concept — not a generic query builder leaking from the database.

cards.title: The Specification Pattern
cards.teaser: A Specification is a composable predicate object that encodes a business rule about whether an object satisfies certain criteria. Combined with a Repository, it enables rich query expressions in domain terms without hardcoding every possible query as a separate method.

runs.text: Evans and Martin Fowler described the Specification pattern as a way to encode business criteria in a reusable, combinable object. The Repository accepts a Specification and returns matching aggregates — the criteria travel as a first-class domain object rather than as a raw query string.
For in-memory implementations the
isSatisfiedBy()
predicate is evaluated directly. For database-backed implementations, a translator converts the Specification into a JPA
Predicate
or Criteria API expression. Spring Data JPA's
JpaSpecificationExecutor
provides exactly this — a
findAll(Specification<T>)
that translates specifications into SQL predicates at query time.

The Specification pattern is powerful but expensive: if the specification can only be evaluated in memory, the Repository may load thousands of aggregates to find the ten that match. Implementations must either translate specs to database predicates or restrict their use to small datasets.

A Specification is a named, combinable business rule you can hand to a Repository: "give me everything matching this criteria." You can AND, OR, and NOT them together without writing a new Repository method for every possible query combination.

cards.title: Repository vs DAO
cards.teaser: A Repository and a Data Access Object (DAO) look similar but serve different masters. The DAO is table-centric — one DAO per table, methods matching database operations. The Repository is aggregate-centric — one Repository per aggregate root, methods matching domain intent.

runs.text: The DAO pattern predates DDD and originates from J2EE. A DAO is a thin object that maps to a persistence artifact — typically a table or a view. It provides
CRUD at the row level
. A Repository provides
semantics at the aggregate level

runs.text: In practice many codebases use DAOs inside Repository implementations. That is fine — DAOs become an implementation detail, hidden behind the Repository interface. The domain only sees the Repository.

If you find yourself calling multiple DAOs in an application service to build a single object before doing domain work, you are doing in the service what a Repository should be doing. Move the assembly inside a Repository implementation.

A DAO is a thin wrapper around a database table — it thinks in rows. A Repository is a domain object that hands you whole aggregates — it thinks in business concepts. You can use DAOs inside a Repository implementation, but domain code should only ever see the Repository.

cards.title: ORM-Repository Tension
cards.teaser: Every major ORM ships with its own repository-like abstraction (JpaRepository, ActiveRecord, Eloquent). Using these directly exposes ORM concepts — lazy loading, sessions, identity maps — to the domain. The tension is about how much persistence leaks through.

runs.text: ORMs and Repository interfaces solve overlapping problems. The friction is real and worth understanding explicitly.

items.text: directly in the domain interface binds the domain to JPA semantics.

— ORMs load associations lazily by default. A Repository that returns a lazily loaded aggregate can trigger session-not-open exceptions in the domain layer once the repository method returns and the persistence session closes.
— ORM sessions maintain an identity map. The Repository's "always reconstitute fully" contract conflicts with the ORM's optimization of returning cached instances.
directly, bypassing the domain-named finder methods and embedding persistence concepts in the service layer.

runs.text: The practical resolution is the
anti-corruption layer approach
: define a domain interface with domain-named methods, and create an infrastructure implementation that delegates to a
JpaRepository
. The domain stays clean; the ORM stays productive.

ORM frameworks like JPA already do repository-like things, but they expose database concepts. The solution is to define a clean domain interface and hide the ORM inside the implementation — domain code sees no JPA, the ORM still does its job.

cards.title: In-Memory Repository for Testing
cards.teaser: An in-memory Repository implementation backed by a plain Map or List is one of the highest-leverage testing tools in DDD. It eliminates database dependencies from unit tests, runs in milliseconds, and exercises the same domain interface as the production implementation.

runs.text: Because the Repository is declared as an interface in the domain layer, a test double is straightforward to build. An in-memory implementation stores aggregates in a
HashMap
and needs no database, no Spring context, and no test containers.
The test suite swaps the production
JpaOrderRepository
for
InMemoryOrderRepository
via constructor injection. All domain logic — aggregate invariants, domain events, service behavior — is verified without a single database round-trip.

items.text: — in-memory tests run in microseconds vs milliseconds for database tests.
— no shared state between test cases if the in-memory store is instantiated fresh per test.
— the test double exercises the real domain interface, not a mock with stubbed expectations.

runs.text: Vernon calls this the "Ubiquitous Unit-Test Enabler." The in-memory Repository is not just a convenience — it is evidence that the Repository interface is correctly designed (infrastructure-free). If you cannot implement it in memory, the interface has leaked persistence.

An in-memory Repository is just a HashMap that implements the same interface as your database-backed one. Your tests use the HashMap version — no database needed — and you know the interface is clean because it was possible to implement it without any database code.

cards.title: Custom Finder Methods
cards.teaser: Beyond findById, Repositories grow custom finders named after domain concepts — findActiveCustomersOver18(), findOrdersPendingShipmentOlderThan(). These are not arbitrary query generators; they encode business intent that would otherwise scatter across service layers.

runs.text: Every business domain has recurring query patterns that carry meaning. Encoding those patterns as named methods on the Repository interface keeps the Ubiquitous Language consistent from the domain model through to the persistence boundary.

cards.title: Pagination and the Repository
cards.teaser: Returning unbounded result sets from a Repository is a production outage waiting to happen. Pagination support — page number/size, cursor-based, or keyset — must be a first-class concern in the interface design, not an afterthought.

runs.text: As data volumes grow, any finder that returns
List<T>
without bounds becomes a risk. A Repository that loads 50,000 aggregates into memory to return them all will degrade or crash under real-world load.

items.text: . Simple to implement, but performance degrades at high offsets due to database-side row scanning. Also susceptible to phantom reads between pages.
. Stable across concurrent inserts, O(1) in terms of rows scanned. Preferred for large datasets and event feeds.
that includes total count, has-next, and current page number is a domain decision — it determines what the caller can show in a UI.

runs.text: Pagination parameters should not be arbitrary integers from UI input. A Repository method should either accept a bounded
Pageable
value object that enforces maximum page size or apply a hard limit internally. Allowing
size=Integer.MAX_VALUE
defeats the purpose.

findAll() returning a bare List<T> is a code smell at any scale above trivial. Add pagination or remove the method entirely and replace it with purpose-built finders that have bounded result sets by design.

A Repository that returns unlimited results will eventually blow up in production. Pagination — either by page number or by cursor — must be built into the interface from the start, not bolted on after the outage.

cards.title: Read Model Bypass — Repositories for Writes, CQRS for Reads
cards.teaser: Repositories are optimized for loading aggregates for command processing. Complex reporting queries — dashboards, search results, analytics — should bypass the repository entirely and read from a dedicated read model. This is the essence of CQRS at the persistence boundary.

runs.text: A fundamental tension in Repository design: the Repository is built to return fully reconstituted aggregates for mutation. But read operations — list views, search results, dashboards — often need projections that span multiple aggregates, join data in ways that violate aggregate boundaries, and require performance characteristics different from write paths.
Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) resolves this by separating the write model (domain model + repositories) from the read model (projections, views, denormalized read stores):

items.text: — application commands load an aggregate via its Repository, invoke domain behavior, and the Repository persists the result. The domain model is fully enforced.

— queries bypass the domain model and Repository entirely. They read from a denormalized projection — a read-optimized table, a materialized view, a search index, or a cache — built by a projection handler subscribed to domain events.

runs.text: The read model has its own query interface, separate from the Repository interface. It is often a thin query service that returns DTOs rather than domain objects:

You do not need full event sourcing to apply the read-model bypass. Even a simple materialized view updated synchronously after each write is a read model. The point is to stop forcing complex queries through the aggregate loading machinery.

Repositories are for loading aggregates to change them. For display, search, and reporting, skip the Repository entirely and query a simpler, flattened read store optimized for those specific reads. That is the read-model bypass.

cards.teaser: Spring Data JpaRepository gives you most of the plumbing for free. Active Record couples persistence to the domain object itself — convenient but harmful to testability. Vernon's and Evans's treatments differ subtly on collection-oriented vs persistence-oriented defaults.

Becomes problematic in complex domains because the domain object imports ORM framework classes, cannot be used without a database connection, and is hard to unit-test in isolation. Active Record is an explicit anti-recommendation for rich domain models.

— favors collection-oriented interfaces with persistence-oriented implementations. Repository interfaces are defined in the domain, implementations in infrastructure, with an explicit anti-corruption layer between ORM entities and domain objects if needed.

— emphasizes that the Repository interface speaks the Ubiquitous Language and that implementation details are free to vary. Evans is less prescriptive about collection vs persistence orientation and more focused on the conceptual role.

runs.text: For most greenfield Spring Boot projects the pragmatic choice is: define a domain-interface in the domain layer, implement it in infrastructure using Spring Data's
JpaRepository
as a delegate, and keep ORM annotations confined to infrastructure-layer entity classes rather than on the domain aggregates themselves.

Active Record is a trap for rich domains. The moment you need to unit-test domain behavior, you will regret coupling the domain object to the ORM. The separation that Repository provides is cheap upfront and invaluable at scale.

Spring Data gives you a Repository for free but leaks JPA details. Active Record is the simplest approach but couples your domain to the database. The DDD way is to hide whichever ORM you use behind a clean domain interface and let infrastructure wire it up.

cards.title: Repository Interface Placement and Dependency Direction
cards.teaser: The Repository interface belongs in the domain layer — not the infrastructure layer. This is a deliberate application of the Dependency Inversion Principle: infrastructure depends on the domain, never the reverse. Getting this wrong couples the domain to the database.

runs.text: In a layered DDD architecture the dependency rule is strict: the domain layer must not import anything from the infrastructure layer. This means Repository
interfaces
live in the domain, and Repository
implementations
live in infrastructure. The direction of the source-code dependency is inverted relative to the runtime call direction.

items.text: contains: aggregate roots, value objects, domain services, repository interfaces, domain events. No infrastructure imports.
contains: command handlers, application services. Depends on domain interfaces. Receives implementations via constructor injection.
contains: repository implementations, ORM entity classes, database migrations, message broker adapters. Imports from domain to implement interfaces.

runs.text: The enforcement mechanism is the package/module boundary, verified at build time via ArchUnit, Checkstyle, or Java module declarations. Without enforcement, the dependency direction drifts within months as developers take shortcuts.

Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters) formalizes the same rule: the Repository interface is a Port (in the domain), and the JPA implementation is an Adapter (in the infrastructure ring). The metaphor differs from layered architecture; the dependency direction is identical.

Put the Repository interface in the domain package and the implementation in the infrastructure package. The domain never imports infrastructure — infrastructure imports the domain interface and implements it. Dependency Inversion keeps the domain clean.
